{{Redirect|White heath|the town|White Heath, Illinois}}{{Short description|Species of flowering plant}} {{Speciesbox | image = Erica arborea JPG1.jpg | genus = Erica | species = arborea | authority = [[Carl Linnaeus|L.]] | range_map = Erica arborea range.svg | range_map_caption = Distribution map |status = LC |status_system = IUCN3.1 |status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Harvey-Brown, Y. |author2=Barstow, M. |date=2017 |title=''Erica arborea'' |volume=2017 |article-number=e.T73094040A109616921 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2017-3.RLTS.T73094040A109616921.en |access-date=19 November 2021}} |synonyms= |synonyms_ref= }} [[File:Erica arborea 12.JPG|thumb|right|''Erica arborea'', Northwest Africa]] '''''Erica arborea''''', the '''tree heath''' or '''tree heather''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] (angiosperms) in the heather family [[Ericaceae]], native to the [[Mediterranean Basin]] and [[Ethiopia]], [[Kenya]] and [[Tanzania]] in [[East Africa]]. It is also cultivated as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]]. The wood, known as '''briar root''' ([[French language|French]]: bruyère, [[Catalan language|Catalan]]: bruc, [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]]: betouro, [[Spanish language|Spanish]]: brezo), is extremely hard and heat-resistant, and is used for making smoking pipes. Leaf fossils attributed to this species were described for the Mio-Pleistocene deposit of São Jorge in Madeira Island.{{Cite journal|last1=Góis-Marques|first1=Carlos A.|last2=Madeira|first2=José|last3=Sequeira|first3=Miguel Menezes de|date=2018-01-26|title=Inventory and review of the Mio–Pleistocene São Jorge flora (Madeira Island, Portugal): palaeoecological and biogeographical implications|journal=Journal of Systematic Palaeontology|volume=16|issue=2|pages=159–177|doi=10.1080/14772019.2017.1282991|bibcode=2018JSPal..16..159G |s2cid=132935444|issn=1477-2019|hdl=10400.13/4191|hdl-access=free}} == Description == ''Erica arborea'' is an upright [[evergreen]] shrub or small tree with a typical height in the wild of some {{convert|7|m|0|abbr=on}}, especially in Africa, but more typically {{convert|1|-|4|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} in gardens. It bears dark green needle-like leaves and numerous small honey-scented bell-shaped white [[flower]]s. It is a [[calcifuge]], preferring acid soil in an open sunny situation.{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|page=1136}} ==Distribution and habitat== The heather has a [[disjunct distribution]], including both sides of the [[Mediterranean basin]], the western [[Caucasus]], tropical eastern African mountains, and the [[Arabian Peninsula]].{{Cite POWO|title=''Erica arborea'' L..|id=328204-1|access-date=2025-10-23|mode=cs1}} Throughout the Mediterranean Basin, its distribution is not continuous, extending from the Atlantic coasts of [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]] to the coast of the [[Black Sea]] in [[Turkey]] and [[Georgia_(country)|Georgia]]. The heather occurs within the Mediterranean [[maquis shrublands]] in semi-arid habitats but can also be found in forest undergrowth up to 1400 m a.s.l. in fresher and more humid environments. It prefers acidic or acidified soils derived from siliceous substrates.Reille, M., Gamisans, J., Andrieu-Ponel, V., De Beaulieu, J. L. (1999). ''The Holocene at Lac de Creno, Corsica, France: a key site for the whole island.'' [[New Phytologist]], 141(2), 291-307. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1469-8137.1999.00343.x 10.1046/j.1469-8137.1999.00343.x]Désamoré, A., Laenen, B., Devos, N., Popp, M., González-Mancebo, J. M., Carine, M. A., Vanderpoorten, A. (2011). ''Out of Africa: north-westwards Pleistocene expansions of the heather'' Erica arborea''.'' [[Journal of Biogeography]], 38(1), 164-176. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2699.2010.02387.x 10.1111/j.1365-2699.2010.02387.x] It is also present in an isolated population in the [[Tibesti Mountains]] ([[Chad]]) in the [[Sahara]], where it occurs at the top of upper montane desert steppe vegetation between 2500 and 3000 m a.s.l.Dinies, M., Schimmel, L., Hoelzmann, P., Kröpelin, S., Darius, F., Neef, R. (2021). ''Holocene high-altitude vegetation dynamics on Emi Koussi, Tibesti mountains (Chad, central Sahara).'' In: Runge, J., Gosling, WD, Lézine, A.-M., Scott, L., (Eds). ''Quaternary Vegetation Dynamics — The African Pollen Database, 1st ed.'' CRC Press, 27-50. DOI: [https://doi.org/10.1201/9781003162766 10.1201/9781003162766] In eastern Africa, it is normally referred to as giant heather. It occurs in the [[Ethiopian Highlands]], in the highest mountains along the [[East African Rift]], from southern [[Uganda]] to northern [[Malawi]]. It is also present in the [[Sarawat Mountains]] in the southwestern Arabian Peninsula, including [[Yemen]] and [[Saudi Arabia]]. In Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, the heather is a constituent of the tropical alpine vegetation, dominating the shrubland above the treeline in mountain areas at altitudes between 3,000 and 4,000 m.
It was previously considered to occur in [[Macaronesia]], but the similar species found there is now treated as a separate species, ''[[Erica canariensis]]''.{{Cite journal |last1=Rivas-Martínez |first1=Salvador |display-authors=etal |date=2011 |title=Mapa de series, geoseries y geopermaseries de vegetación de España Parte II |journal=Itinera Geobotánica |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=425–800 |url=https://floramontiberica.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/itinerageobotanica_182_2011.pdf |access-date=2025-10-23 |language=es}}, p. 484 Naturalised populations occur [[Great Britain]], and in south-eastern [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]], where tree heath is seen as a potential environmental weed.*Noble, M. R. (2016). [http://www.caws.org.au/awc/2016/awc201612121.pdf ''The weed potential of ''Erica'' species for Tasmania and other areas of southern Australia''.] 20th Australasian Weeds Conference, 11-15 September 2016, Perth, Western Australia. ==Cultivars== ''Erica arborea'' was being cultivated as early as 1658.{{cite book |author1=Brian Proudley |author2=Valerie Proudley |title=Heathers in Colour |date=1989 |publisher=Blandford Press |isbn=0-7137-1420-4 |page=15 |edition=2nd |quote=Heathers as garden plants have a surprisingly long history. The valuable winter-flowering ''Erica carnea'' was, according to the Royal Horticultural Society's ''Dictionary of Gardening'', introduced into cultivation in this country as long ago as 1763 and the 'Tree heather' ''E. arborea'' ... even earlier in 1658.}} Several [[cultivars]] and [[Hybrid (biology)#Hybrid plants|hybrid]]s have been developed for garden use, of which the following have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 35 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 6 February 2018}} *''E. arborea'' 'Estrella Gold'{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Erica arborea'' 'Estrella Gold'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94614/Erica-arborea-Estrella-Gold/Details | access-date = 7 June 2020}} (gold-tipped leaves) *''E. arborea'' [[variety (botany)|var.]] ''alpina''{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Erica arborea'' var. ''alpina''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/89372/Erica-arborea-var-alpina/Details | access-date = 7 June 2020}} *''E. arborea'' var. ''aureifolia'' 'Albert's Gold'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/59387/Erica-arborea-var-alpina-f-aureifolia-Albert-s-Gold/Details | access-date = 7 June 2020}} (gold-leaved) *''E.'' × ''veitchii'' 'Gold Tips'{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/90226/Erica-x-veitchii-Gold-Tips/Details | title = ''Erica'' × ''veitchii'' 'Gold Tips' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 7 June 2020}} (''E. arborea'' × ''E. lusitanica'') Other tall growing heaths, including the Portugal heath (''[[Erica lusitanica]]'') and channel heath (''[[Erica canaliculata]]'') may also sometimes be called tree heath. ==Uses== [[File:smoking pipe rack.jpg|thumb|170px|right|Briar pipes on a circular pipe rack]] The [[wood]], known as ''briar root'', is extremely hard, dense and heat-resistant, and is primarily used for making [[Tobacco pipe#Briar|smoking pipes]], as it does not affect the aroma of tobacco. The football-sized [[tubers]] are harvested at the age of 30 to 60 years. They are cooked for several hours, then dried for several months before they are further processed.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}} The wood is also used for making jewellery, fountain pens and knife handles.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}} ==See also== * [[Mediterranean forests, woodlands, and scrub]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commonscat}} * Adams, W.M., A.S.
